items.title: When fruits and veggies are scarce, monkeys hunt for meat
items.desc: Capuchin monkeys hunt prey when fruits and vegetables become scarce, potentially mirroring the habits of human ancestors, according to a study published in PLOS One by Susana Carvalho (Gorongosa National Park, Mozambique), Noemi Spagnoletti (Sapienza University of Rome, Italy) and colleagues.

items.title: Climate change exposes up to 560 million children globally to at least one additional month of dangerous heat per year
items.desc: New research by Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) shows that globally, up to 560 million children ages 0–9 (43% of all children in this age group) experience at least one additional month (30 or more days) of heat stress per year because of human-induced climate change. This exposure outpaces that of any other age group and is nearly triple the 190 million people (30%) ages 60–69 experiencing this additional health threat. Children are therefore already facing disproportionately high levels of dangerous humid heat caused by human-induced climate change, with exposure expected to grow under furt

items.title: Many workplaces resist plant-based lunches despite substantial climate benefits
items.desc: Are organizations ready for plant-based food at work? A new study from the University of Copenhagen explores this question and shows that only a small proportion of workplaces in Denmark are ready for this change—despite its potential to reduce the climate footprint of workplace lunches. In general, introducing plant-based food is likely to stir strong emotions.

items.title: Tiny atomic changes could lead to smarter wireless technology
items.desc: Researchers at Queen Mary University of London have shown that making extremely small changes to the structure of a material can dramatically improve its ability to respond to electrical signals. Published recently in Science Advances, the breakthrough could help create a new generation of wireless devices that can change frequency on demand, making communication systems more flexible and energy efficient.

items.title: Narwhals help researchers uncover unique data from the deepest East Greenland fjords
items.desc: They live in some of the most inaccessible waters on Earth, where ocean temperatures hover around freezing. Because they move through areas that humans rarely reach, they have been able to help researchers with a special task.

items.title: Chagas parasite's survival trick offers antimalarial-style target
items.desc: Researchers at the University of Cincinnati have identified a potential new target to prevent the spread of Chagas disease. The parasitic infection is transmitted through the bite of the kissing bug in Central and South America and, more recently, in the United States.

items.title: Buried underwear shows land use is key to soil health
items.desc: Soil is the foundation of our food supply. It stores water, carbon and nutrients and is home to a large share of the world's biodiversity. More than half of global biodiversity is estimated to live below ground. Yet biodiversity, and with it soil health, is declining worldwide, with consequences for agriculture, food security and the functioning of entire ecosystems.

items.title: Did ocean motion carve Enceladus's tiger stripes?
items.desc: Saturn's moon Enceladus sports a thick shell of ice surrounding a liquid water ocean. As though scraped by an enormous claw, four parallel cracks slash across its south pole. Each about 500 meters (1,600 feet) deep, 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) across and 130 kilometers (81 miles) long, the fissures spew water vapor and other materials from the subsurface ocean directly into space. But the origin of these "tiger stripes" is mysterious.

items.title: Even protected Florida wetlands can't escape microplastic pollution
items.desc: Microplastics are turning up almost everywhere—from oceans and rivers to soils and sediments—yet far less is known about what happens when they enter freshwater wetlands. Often overlooked in favor of marine and coastal environments, wetlands can act as both pathways and traps for microplastics, potentially capturing and retaining pollution.

items.title: How high scores in an online brain teaser made mathematicians lie for three years
items.desc: It might not yet be the phenomenon that is Wordle, but for hundreds of thousands of players, Digit Party has scratched the itch of a casual brain teaser to break up their day.

items.title: Congo Basin study reveals nuanced relationship between people and flooding
items.desc: In the Lac Télé Community Reserve, a vast tropical peatland in Africa's Congo Basin that is home to about 20,000 people, the forces of climate change and globalization are hitting residents hard. The seasonal floods upon which village communities have long relied are arriving earlier, staying longer and pushing farther into places that used to remain dry. And these impacts vary dramatically from one village to the next, a new Yale-led study finds.

items.title: Expert Comment: More extreme weather is coming—AI may help us to better prepare for it
items.desc: As of August 2026, the world is bracing for what forecasters describe as one of the strongest El Niño events on record. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) Climate Prediction Center has put the chance of a very strong event this fall and winter above 90%, with a 69% likelihood that it will exceed every El Niño since 1950.

items.title: Reconstructed Jurassic insect calls evoke a 165-million-year-old forest soundscape
items.desc: The sights and sounds of the Jurassic era are long gone, and we will never know for sure what that ancient world looked and sounded like. Fossils can offer clues, and reconstructions can give us a sense of the noises some animals might have made. Now scientists have turned their attention to insects and reconstructed the calls of Jurassic relatives of modern-day crickets and katydids (grasshopper-like insects).

items.title: Looking into the eyes of gibbons: New noninvasive eye-tracking study features these little-studied apes
items.desc: When you look at someone, you usually look at their face. It serves as one of the most important sources of social information in primates, so the evolution of face perception has attracted considerable scientific attention. While an abundance of this research has centered on humans and other great apes, very little has focused on gibbons.

items.title: Gambling branding dominates Premier League YouTube highlights, new study finds
items.desc: New research from the University of Nottingham has found that gambling brands were visible in 32% of Premier League soccer highlight footage, compared with less than 2% of FIFA World Cup highlights, raising questions about viewers' exposure to gambling marketing.

items.title: Scientists may have found a shortcut to calorie restriction’s anti-aging benefits
items.desc: Moderate calorie restriction lowered an immune protein called C3 that appears to help drive chronic inflammation as the body ages. Blocking the same protein reduced age related inflammation in mice, raising the possibility that future treatments could mimic some benefits of calorie restriction without severe dieting.

items.title: Manhattan-sized ice island breaks off Greenland’s Petermann Glacier
items.desc: A Manhattan-sized ice island has broken away from Greenland’s Petermann Glacier after years of growing fractures weakened its floating ice tongue. Scientists expect two more huge sections could soon detach, potentially removing about 22 percent of the remaining ice tongue.

items.title: 190-year-old DNA reveals a hidden pangolin species
items.desc: DNA from a nearly 190-year-old museum specimen has helped scientists confirm a distinct Himalayan pangolin species hiding in plain sight in Nepal and northern India. The discovery could give conservationists a powerful new way to trace illegally traded pangolin scales back to the species and regions being targeted by poachers.

items.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope is ready to hunt thousands of alien worlds
items.desc: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope is now enclosed inside its Falcon Heavy fairing and nearly ready for launch. Its mission could uncover thousands of exoplanets while helping scientists investigate dark matter, dark energy, and the accelerating expansion of the universe.

items.title: Common medications may change your gut for years
items.desc: Common medications may reshape the gut microbiome long after the last dose is taken. In a study of more than 2,500 people, researchers found lasting microbial changes linked not only to antibiotics, but also to antidepressants, beta-blockers, acid-reducing drugs, and benzodiazepines. Some effects were still detectable years later, suggesting past medication use may strongly influence the gut bacteria people carry today.

items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
items.desc: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

items.title: Three forgotten kings could rewrite the history of ancient Assyria
items.desc: Three forgotten Assyrian kings may have been hiding in plain sight for more than 2,700 years. By piecing together clues from tablets, inscriptions, and an ancient statue, researchers argue that these rulers were omitted from the famous Assyrian King List.

items.title: Bird flu is spreading. Your backyard feeder could make it worse
items.desc: Backyard bird feeders could become unexpected hotspots for H5N1 as Australia’s bird flu outbreak spreads, bringing species together in ways that rarely occur naturally. Experts say stopping feeding is safest, while smaller amounts of food, no hand-feeding, and careful cleaning can reduce the danger.

items.title: One asteroid strike may explain two mysteries of Mars’ moon Deimos
items.desc: A single asteroid impact may explain two of Deimos’s most puzzling features: its huge southern depression and unusually smooth, dusty surface. Simulations suggest a roughly 320-meter asteroid struck the Martian moon at an angle, throwing debris around the entire world without breaking it apart. New observations from ESA’s Hera spacecraft support the scenario and indicate that Deimos is surprisingly porous and fragile.

items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
items.desc: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

items.title: Too much or too little sleep may make your body age faster
items.desc: Both too little and too much sleep may be linked to faster aging throughout the body. Researchers analyzing 23 biological aging clocks found the lowest aging levels among people sleeping about 6.4 to 7.8 hours per day. Short or long sleep was also associated with numerous conditions affecting the brain, heart, lungs, metabolism, and digestive system.

items.title: Forces deep inside Earth helped Antarctica freeze before the Arctic
items.desc: Scientists may have solved the mystery of why Antarctica froze millions of years before the Arctic. Slow-moving waves deep inside Earth gradually lifted East Antarctica, building mountains and a high plateau where snow and ice could survive even in a much warmer world. Once glaciers took hold, their bright surfaces reflected sunlight and helped cool the region further.

items.title: Screen time at ages 1 and 6 may matter more than parents realize
items.desc: More screen time during infancy and around the start of school was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later. The findings suggest that early childhood may contain particularly sensitive windows when screen habits can have longer-lasting effects.

items.title: Childhood trauma may leave a lasting “scar” inside brain cells
items.desc: Early-life stress may physically alter how DNA is packaged in the brain, leaving stress-related genes primed to activate more easily years later. In mice, researchers were able to block this effect, preventing the heightened anxiety and stress sensitivity that otherwise appeared in adulthood.

items.title: Your brain may not actually “make” decisions
items.desc: A neuroscientist is challenging the idea that the brain contains a central system that actually “makes” our decisions. What we experience as choosing may instead emerge from the continuous interaction of perception, movement, the body, and the world around us.

items.title: The Economist’s Embarrassing Proxy War Over AI Policy
items.desc: The disagreements between the Nobel laureate economist Daron Acemoglu and his opponents are consequential—and so are the opponents. But rather than engage in good faith with Acemoglu's arguments, the venerable British news magazine recently stooped to bibulous calumny by unnamed critics of his work.

items.title: Democracies Must Get Serious About Industrial Policy
items.desc: For decades, Western governments have ceded the strategic direction of their economies to the market. To dominate the industries of the future, they must learn from their own history and rebuild the institutions, expertise, and discipline that effective industrial policy demands.

items.title: In the AI Gold Rush, the Cloud Wins
items.desc: Even if the AI investment boom turns out to have been a bubble, the Big Tech companies that have cornered the cloud infrastructure market will emerge as strong as ever, or even stronger. That is why Amazon, Microsoft, and Google are in a league of their own, even compared to other giants like Meta and Nvidia.

items.title: Don’t Mess With Markets
items.desc: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has justified his intervention in currency and bond markets by arguing that they are not providing a fair signal of economic fundamentals. But they are, and Bessent's willingness to peddle such nonsense may be the most striking testament yet to the sycophancy that defines the Trump administration.

items.title: Kevin Warsh Owes Us an Apology
items.desc: After only a few months in office, the chair of the US Federal Reserve has left market participants disoriented and confused. His first address to the annual monetary-policy symposium in Jackson Hole is an opportunity to set things aright—or to make matters even worse.

items.title: Is the Trump Treasury Panicking?
items.desc: With the federal deficit near 6% of GDP and the national debt surpassing $40 trillion, America’s fiscal position looks increasingly precarious. By trying to strong-arm the bond market rather than address the underlying problem, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent may have squandered his hard-earned credibility.

items.title: What the World’s Oldest Bank Reveals About EU Financial Integration
items.desc: To fend off an attempted takeover, Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena has launched its own bids for two other Italian banks. The episode shows why EU policymakers should focus less on making governments surrender their influence over national banking systems and more on building a European financing channel.

items.title: The Age of Gated Recessions
items.desc: Aggregate economic indicators are obscuring a widening divide between those enjoying rapid income growth and those facing deteriorating job prospects. The rise of AI could deepen this disparity, with certain regions and workers experiencing recession-like conditions while others enjoy boom times.

items.title: The AI Curse
items.desc: Every sanction that ordinary citizens have ever possessed—the ability to withhold labor, taxes, sons, or votes—presupposes someone who needs what you can withhold. As AI infrastructure encroaches on Americans, they are learning the lesson of many resource-rich states: where there is no need, there is no democracy.

items.title: Where Will the Global Bond Rout Hit Growth and Equities?
items.desc: In the US, the recent rise in bond yields is largely driven by structural factors like the end of the post-2008 Great Stagnation, higher potential growth from tech-industry investments, and greater private-sector demand for credit. Higher yields are more worrisome for advanced economies that are stagnating and innovating less.

items.title: Trump’s Korean Catastrophe
items.desc: Donald Trump seems not to appreciate that deterrence depends on the ability to mount a credible defense. This makes the Korean Peninsula a more dangerous place, not least because 28,000 US troops are stationed in South Korea, which the US is obliged by treaty to defend.

items.title: The Dollar’s Outer Defenses Have Been Breached
items.desc: The puzzle of why the Trump administration is so concerned with a falling yen has historical parallels not to the 1930s or the 1980s, but to the 1960s, when US officials feared that a crisis elsewhere could spread to America. With US bond yields spiking, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is getting desperate.

items.title: Why the World Still Needs Wall Street
items.desc: Outside of the United States, all other financial systems face major constraints on their ability to absorb large financial inflows. That is why geopolitical multipolarity is advancing faster than financial multipolarity, despite the many reasons that investors have to pursue greater diversification.

items.title: Aging Populations Need Not Mean Frailer Economies
items.desc: Governments and economists have long viewed demographic aging as a threat to economic growth. But new research finds that labor scarcity encourages investment and shifts innovation toward labor-saving technologies, boosting productivity enough to offset a shrinking workforce.

items.title: Who’s Afraid of Chinese Surpluses?
items.desc: China recorded the largest trade surplus in history last year, and its exports continue to grow. But the scale of the threat to the global economy, and the appropriate response, remains subject to considerable disagreement. Some economists advocate protectionist measures, if only to pressure China to commit to economic rebalancing, others argue that tariffs won’t help, and still others think the specter of another “China shock” is a bogeyman, because China’s surpluses do more good than harm.
